summary: A Best Current Practice document that defines how media feature tags are registered, using IANA as the central registry for the media feature vocabulary. It lets different systems describe their capabilities with a shared set of names.

plainLanguage.summary: Media feature tags give systems shared names for capabilities that affect how content can be presented. RFC 2506 defines how tags are written and reviewed, and provides a URI-based option that needs no registration.

subtitle: How media feature tags describe capabilities and how new tags enter the shared registry.

tldr.problem: Systems that exchange content need shared names for capabilities and preferences, such as display or printing features.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines media feature tags, their syntax and value types, three registration trees, and a template for proposals reviewed by IANA or the IESG.
tldr.outcome: Tags in the URI tree can be defined without registration. RFC 2506 is Best Current Practice BCP 31.

today: RFC 2506 is Best Current Practice BCP 31, published in March 1999. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Shared Vocabulary for Capabilities
sections.content:
Internet applications connect different data formats, platforms, and communities. They need a common vocabulary to describe capabilities and preferences so that systems can match content to the receiving party.

RFC 2506 establishes IANA as a central registry for media feature tags and defines a URI tree for sharing definitions without registration.
sections.plainLanguage: Systems need consistent names for features such as screen color or available paper. A shared vocabulary helps them describe and compare those capabilities.

sections.title: What a Media Feature Tag Describes
sections.content:
A media feature tag names one simple characteristic related to media capability or a resource's properties. Examples include screen color depth, printer paper, available fonts, and the ability to display graphics.

Each tag has one data type. Larger descriptions, such as display width and height, combine several individual tags. MIME media types must not be registered as feature tags.
sections.plainLanguage: Each tag describes one capability or preference and has one defined kind of value. A larger description can combine multiple tags.

sections.title: Tag Names and Values
sections.content:
A tag uses US-ASCII letters, digits, colon, slash, dot, percent, and dash. Tags are case-insensitive and should begin with a letter. Dots may mark parts of a hierarchy.

The registry supports signed integers, rational numbers, tokens with equality or ordering rules, and strings with defined comparison rules. A tag's registration states one value type and defines any comparison or unit needed to interpret it.
sections.plainLanguage: A tag uses a restricted set of keyboard characters and has one defined value type. Measurements use a canonical unit so systems can compare them consistently.

sections.title: Three Registration Trees
sections.content:
The IETF tree holds tags of general Internet interest and requires IESG approval and publication of the specification as an RFC. The global tree uses names beginning with g. and requires review by a designated expert.

The URI tree uses names beginning with u. followed by a URI. Its URI author is the authority for the definition, and these tags are considered unregistered under this procedure. IANA may create additional top-level trees with IESG advice and consent.
sections.plainLanguage: The three trees have different review rules. IETF tags receive formal standards review, global tags receive expert review, and URI tags rely on their URI definition without registration.

sections.title: Submitting a Registration
sections.content:
IANA registers an IETF-tree tag after the IESG confirms approval. A global-tree tag is registered after a designated expert checks that it meets the technical requirements.

The registration template asks for the name, meaning, value type, intended use, contact, change controller, and security considerations. A proposal may request a publication delay of up to two months for IETF and global tree tags; that delay does not stop mailing-list discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: A proposal states what the tag means, what values it accepts, and who maintains it. The review path depends on which registration tree the tag uses.

sections.title: Privacy and Capability Disclosure
sections.content:
Negotiation mechanisms can reveal information about one party to other parties. That information may raise privacy concerns and may help a malicious party guess which security weaknesses are present.

The RFC includes security considerations in the registration template so a proposer can describe privacy and denial-of-service concerns related to incorrect values.
sections.plainLanguage: Sharing capabilities can reveal information about a device or its software. A registration should describe relevant privacy and security concerns.
